articles.title: After US-China tariff deal, will orders shift away from Vietnam? - news.tuoitre.vn
articles.summary: After US-China tariff deal, will orders shift away from Vietnam?  news.tuoitre.vn
articles.full_text:
Speaking to Tuoi Tre (Youth) online newspaper, Rizwan Khan, managing partner at investment consultancy Acclime Vietnam, said the latest tariff reductions cover only a limited share of bilateral trade.
Around US$60 billion worth of goods is covered by the tariff-reduction mechanism, accounting for about 14 percent of U.S.-China trade in 2025.
Of this, some $30 billion worth of Chinese goods could see lower U.S. tariffs, equivalent to 9.7 percent of China’s exports to the U.S..
The average U.S. tariff on Chinese goods would also fall only modestly, from about 22 percent to 20.5 percent, still nearly double the 11 percent level recorded in early 2025.
Short-term pressure on orders
Khan said most of the products covered are non-sensitive goods, but some categories are important to Vietnam, including toys, plastics, and household products.
These are low-margin, highly price-sensitive industries, meaning even a small tariff difference can affect sourcing decisions.
“Some U.S. buyers may shift part of their short-term orders back to existing suppliers in China, particularly for products whose tariffs return to most-favored-nation levels,” he said.
Still, Khan said the impact is more likely to emerge through order volumes and price negotiations over the next few quarters than through factory relocation.
For multinational companies, moving production is a long-term decision involving investment cycles of 10 to 20 years and substantial costs in supplier networks, logistics, and labor.
The tariff changes therefore have some significance, he said, but they are not broad enough to fundamentally alter the investment logic behind China+1, the business strategy of avoiding investing only in China or sourcing only from China.
Investors will also wait for clarity on final tariff rates, product coverage, and the duration of the reductions, as well as U.S. rules on origin and transshipment, Vietnam-U.S. trade negotiations and the tariff gap between China and alternative manufacturing bases.
Khan said China+1 remains a broader strategy aimed at reducing supply-chain concentration and geopolitical risk, rather than merely a response to tariffs.
Vietnam urged to strengthen domestic value
For Vietnam, Khan said a key priority is to conclude a reciprocal trade arrangement with the U.S. and address concerns raised by Washington, including non-tariff barriers.
Vietnam could also help ease concerns over its bilateral trade surplus by increasing purchases of U.S. products where there is genuine demand, such as agricultural goods, liquefied natural gas, and aircraft.
Rules of origin are another key issue.
As the U.S. steps up scrutiny of tariff evasion and transshipment, Vietnam will need stronger systems to verify where goods come from and how much processing takes place domestically.
Khan suggested digitizing certificates of origin, increasing oversight of projects at risk of being used mainly for transshipment, and improving supply-chain traceability, including compliance with U.S. forced-labor requirements.
He also said Vietnam needs to raise the share of value created at home.
Many manufacturing sectors still depend heavily on imported components and raw materials. In electronics, for example, industry estimates put the localization rate at only around 15-20 percent.
Building stronger domestic Tier-1 and Tier-2 supplier networks would help Vietnam retain more value and reduce its reliance on imported inputs.
“The goal should not simply be to attract another factory, but to build the capabilities of suppliers and supporting industries around that factory,” Khan said.
Beyond a manufacturing base
Human resources and energy will also become increasingly important as the next wave of China+1 investment moves into more advanced industries.
Future projects will require technical workers in semiconductor design and testing, automation and supply-chain management, as well as better access to renewable energy.
For Vietnam, Khan said the opportunity is therefore no longer just about absorbing production leaving China.
“The more important question is not whether China+1 will continue, but whether Vietnam can move from being an alternative manufacturing location to becoming an increasingly integrated and higher-value link in global supply chains,” he said.
U.S.-China tariff deal
The U.S. and China agreed in late September to reduce tariffs on about $30 billion worth of non-sensitive goods in each direction following Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington.
According to the White House, the agreement covers U.S. exports to China such as agricultural products, wood, and cosmetics, while Chinese exports to the U.S. include small appliances, toys, and decorations.
The two sides described the deal as a consensus on recommendations for more favorable tariff treatment, rather than a blanket tariff cut across all bilateral trade.

articles.title: Vietnam Posts Near-Double-Digit Quarterly Growth on Manufacturing Surge - briefasia.com
articles.summary: Vietnam Posts Near-Double-Digit Quarterly Growth on Manufacturing Surge  briefasia.com
articles.full_text:
Quarterly Acceleration Marks Four-Year High
Vietnam's economy expanded 9.95 per cent in the three months ending September 2026, according to data released by the National Statistics Office. The figure represents an uptick from 8.81 per cent recorded in the April-June quarter and marks the strongest quarterly performance the country has delivered since the third quarter of 2022.
For the first nine months of the calendar year, cumulative growth reached 9.01 per cent, the fastest January-September pace Vietnam has registered in 15 years. The figures underscore the momentum behind the government's stated ambition to sustain double-digit expansion across the next five-year planning cycle.
The quarterly acceleration was underpinned by a sharp rise in trade volumes. Merchandise exports climbed 24.5 per cent on a year-on-year basis, while import growth reached 36.7 per cent over the same period. The import surge reflects heightened demand for intermediate goods and capital equipment, much of it destined for electronics assembly plants and textile factories clustered in the country's industrial zones.
Manufacturing Backbone and Foreign Capital
Vietnam's industrial base has become a critical node in regional supply chains, particularly for electronics, garments, and footwear. Multinational corporations have steadily expanded capacity in the country, drawn by competitive labour costs, improving infrastructure, and a network of free-trade agreements that grant preferential access to major markets.
Foreign direct investment has remained robust throughout 2026, continuing a trend that has defined Vietnam's development model for more than a decade. Capital inflows have been channelled primarily into manufacturing and export-oriented sectors, reinforcing the country's position as a production hub for global brands seeking alternatives to higher-cost locations elsewhere in the region.
The Asian Development Bank revised its full-year 2026 GDP forecast for Vietnam upward in late September, lifting the projection to 7.8 per cent from an earlier estimate of 7.2 per cent published in July. The upgrade cited continued expansion in manufacturing output, resilient household consumption, and the steady flow of foreign investment as key drivers.
Domestic consumption has held up despite elevated inflation in certain food categories and rising borrowing costs. Retail sales growth has been supported by wage increases in the formal sector and remittance inflows from the Vietnamese diaspora, which have helped sustain purchasing power in urban and peri-urban areas.
Tariff Resilience and Market Dynamics
Vietnam recorded 8 per cent annual growth in 2025, a performance that placed it among the fastest-growing economies globally. That expansion came even as the United States, Vietnam's largest single export destination, imposed additional tariffs on certain product categories. The country's export sector demonstrated resilience by diversifying shipment destinations and shifting product mix toward higher-value items.
The ability to maintain export momentum in the face of tariff headwinds reflects the depth of integration Vietnam has achieved within multinational supply chains. Companies with established operations in the country have been reluctant to relocate, given the sunk costs in plant and equipment and the trained workforce available locally.
In September 2026, FTSE Russell upgraded Vietnam's stock market to secondary emerging market status, a reclassification that is expected to attract additional portfolio inflows from institutional investors tracking benchmark indices. The upgrade followed years of regulatory reforms aimed at improving market liquidity, transparency, and foreign-ownership limits.
The equity market reclassification is likely to increase foreign participation in Vietnamese equities, particularly in the banking, consumer, and industrial sectors. Portfolio managers have noted that Vietnamese stocks trade at a valuation discount relative to regional peers, offering potential upside for investors willing to navigate a market still characterised by relatively thin liquidity in certain counters.
Headwinds on the Horizon
Despite the strong performance through the first three quarters, the Asian Development Bank flagged potential headwinds in its September forecast update. Weaker global demand, particularly in advanced economies grappling with monetary tightening and subdued consumer sentiment, poses a risk to Vietnam's export-dependent growth model.
Geopolitical uncertainty remains another variable. Trade tensions, export controls on technology components, and shifting tariff regimes in major markets could disrupt supply chains and dampen investor confidence. Vietnam's reliance on imported inputs for its export industries means that any disruption to regional logistics networks or escalation in trade disputes would have direct consequences for production schedules and shipment volumes.
Domestically, policymakers face the challenge of balancing growth objectives with macroeconomic stability. Rapid credit expansion has raised concerns about asset quality in the banking sector, while inflation pressures in food and energy have eroded real incomes for lower-income households. The government has signalled its intention to maintain an accommodative fiscal stance while tightening oversight of lending practices in the property sector, where speculative activity has driven up prices in major cities.
Regional Context and Outlook
Vietnam's growth trajectory stands out in a regional context marked by uneven performance. While several Southeast Asian economies have struggled with slower export demand and weakening currencies, Vietnam has maintained its appeal as a destination for manufacturing investment and a reliable supplier to global markets.
The country's ability to attract capital and sustain export growth hinges on continued improvements in infrastructure, skills development, and regulatory predictability. Transport bottlenecks, power supply constraints, and bureaucratic delays remain pain points for foreign investors, and addressing these issues will be critical to sustaining the growth rates the government is targeting.
Looking ahead, the trajectory of Vietnam's economy will depend on how effectively policymakers manage external shocks while maintaining the investment climate that has underpinned the country's rise as a manufacturing hub. The near-term outlook remains positive, but sustaining momentum will require navigating a global environment that has grown more uncertain and fragmented.

articles.title: Vietnam Posts 9.95% GDP Growth in Third Quarter - briefasia.com
articles.summary: Vietnam Posts 9.95% GDP Growth in Third Quarter  briefasia.com
articles.full_text:
Industrial Momentum Lifts Growth
Vietnam's economy expanded 9.95 per cent year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026, according to the National Statistics Office. The July-September figure represents the strongest quarterly performance this year, outpacing the 8.15 per cent and 8.81 per cent growth recorded in the first and second quarters respectively.
The acceleration brought nine-month cumulative growth to 9.01 per cent, with industry-construction and services sectors contributing 45 per cent and 49.6 per cent of the expansion. The industrial segment grew 11.21 per cent as large-scale projects commenced operations, export activity recovered and public investment disbursement gained pace.
Services rose 8.69 per cent on robust domestic consumption across retail, hospitality and tourism. Agriculture, forestry and seafood production added 4.02 per cent growth.
Investment Flows Accelerate
Total realised investment at current prices reached approximately VND3.11 quadrillion ($119.7 billion) in the first nine months, up 15.1 per cent year-on-year. Non-state entities accounted for 53 per cent of the total, reflecting continued private sector confidence.
Foreign direct investment inflows showed particularly strong momentum. Registered FDI, including new capital, adjustments and equity transactions, climbed 76.4 per cent to $50.36 billion. Realised FDI rose 12.1 per cent to $21.07 billion, the highest level in five years.
The surge in committed capital suggests multinational manufacturers continue to view Vietnam as a priority destination for supply chain diversification, particularly in electronics and machinery production.
Trade Deficit Emerges
Import-export turnover exceeded $888 billion in the nine-month period, a 30.4 per cent increase. Imports jumped 36.7 per cent to $453.72 billion, while exports advanced 24.5 per cent to $434.3 billion.
The differential resulted in a trade deficit of $19.42 billion, reversing the $16.87 billion surplus recorded in the same period last year. The shift reflects rising imports of capital goods and components for manufacturing expansion, as well as increased consumer goods purchases driven by domestic demand.
Inflation and Business Dynamics
Consumer price inflation averaged 4.52 per cent in the first three quarters compared to the prior year, with core inflation at 4.26 per cent. The figures indicate price pressures remain elevated but manageable.
Business formation data presented a mixed picture. More than 223,900 enterprises were newly established or resumed operations during the period, down 3.2 per cent year-on-year. Nearly 89,800 businesses temporarily suspended operations, while 33,500 awaited dissolution. Over 48,700 firms completed dissolution procedures, up 118.8 per cent.
The uptick in closures reflects ongoing restructuring as smaller operators struggle with financing costs and competitive pressure.
Path to Double-Digit Growth
Nguyen Thi Huong, director of the National Statistics Office, acknowledged that while third-quarter growth significantly exceeded previous years, achieving double-digit expansion for the full year remains challenging.
Vietnam is targeting full-year growth above 10 per cent. International forecasts have been more conservative: the Asian Development Bank, UOB, the International Monetary Fund and Standard Chartered projected 2026 growth between 7.5 per cent and 9.5 per cent.
The statistics office recommended maintaining macroeconomic stability and inflation control while pursuing growth objectives. Priority measures include accelerating public investment disbursement, removing production bottlenecks, strengthening export capacity among domestic firms and stimulating consumer demand.
Authorities also flagged the need to monitor external risks, including Middle East conflicts, oil price volatility, transportation costs and exchange rate movements. These factors could influence import costs and export competitiveness in the final quarter, particularly for manufacturing sectors reliant on global supply chains.
The trajectory of public investment disbursement will likely determine whether Vietnam can sustain momentum through year-end. Historical patterns show fourth-quarter disbursement typically accelerates as agencies rush to meet annual targets, providing a potential tailwind for construction and infrastructure-linked sectors.

articles.title: Vietnam needs 12.5% GDP growth for Q4 to hit double-digit annual target: PM - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Vietnam needs 12.5% GDP growth for Q4 to hit double-digit annual target: PM  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Vietnam needs economic growth of more than 12.5% in the fourth quarter to achieve its target of double-digit GDP growth for the full year, Prime Minister Le Minh Hung said at a government meeting on Saturday.
"This is very significant pressure and a very challenging task, requiring ministries, sectors and localities to show the highest level of determination and effort," he added.
The country's Q3 growth reached 9.95% and nine-month growth hit 9.01%, the highest since 2011. The index of industrial production (IIP) rose 12.2% in the first nine months, also the strongest pace in many years, the National Statistics Office reported.
According to the government, the macroeconomy remains broadly stable, inflation is under control and major economic balances are secured, while monetary, fiscal and other macroeconomic policies are being coordinated in a proactive and effective manner amid heavy pressure from global fuel markets and strong demand for capital from the economy.
Despite the overall positive results, PM Hung pointed to several difficulties and challenges. Macroeconomic management is facing growing pressure, while high growth has yet to meet the target and inflationary pressures remain significant. Some localities and growth drivers have underperformed expectations, while traditional growth drivers have not been fully harnessed.
Interest rates remain relatively high, while businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, continue to face difficulties accessing capital and credit. Some long-standing projects have yet to be fully resolved. The country also recorded a relatively large trade deficit in the first nine months.
Hung ordered ministries and local authorities to closely control prices and strive to keep average consumer price inflation in 2026 in line with the target set by the National Assembly, at about 4.5%. The instruction came as average CPI rose 4.52% in the first nine months amid strong pressure from higher global fuel prices.
He instructed authorities not to raise electricity prices and to continue studying appropriate measures to manage electricity and fuel prices. Local authorities were told to manage prices of goods in their areas, while ministries and agencies must ensure adequate supplies of essential goods such as food, construction materials and medicines.
Authorities must also step up inspections and strictly handle hoarding, speculation and smuggling, he stressed.
Electricity output reached 266.2 billion kilowatt-hours in the first nine months, up 9.5% from a year earlier, Minister of Industry and Trade Le Manh Hung said. In Q4, the ministry would continue to tap domestic primary energy sources, reduce reliance on imported oil, gas and coal, coordinate hydropower reservoir operations and prepare for El Nino.
The prime minister instructed the Ministry of Industry and Trade and businesses to ensure adequate supplies of electricity and fuel. The ministry must soon submit and implement the adjusted Power Development Plan VIII and restructure state utility EVN. It must also complete and submit a decree on fuel trading and increase coal and oil and gas production.
The ministry was ordered to prepare a plan to implement the reciprocal trade agreement as soon as it is signed, while accelerating measures to boost exports, control the trade defici, and develop balanced and sustainable trade.
It must also help businesses respond to changes in international trade, make use of next-generation free trade agreements, step up trade promotion, diversify export markets, and stimulate domestic demand.
The prime minister instructed the Ministry of Finance to urgently submit for immediate government approval a decree cutting income tax by 30% for businesses and household businesses with annual revenue of no more than VND10 billion ($384,830). The ministry must also focus on simplifying tax administration and procedures related to public investment.

articles.title: South-east Asia among economies most vulnerable to AI correction, Asean unit warns - The Business Times
articles.summary: South-east Asia among economies most vulnerable to AI correction, Asean unit warns  The Business Times
articles.full_text:
The region is ‘particularly exposed’ as it is at the centre of global AI supply chains, says report
[SINGAPORE] South-east Asia, together with China, Japan and South Korea, is more at risk than most economies to any potential collapse in the artificial intelligence boom, which could trigger shocks across financial markets and the real economy.
The region is “particularly exposed” because it is at the centre of global AI supply chains and “increasingly integrated into AI-related financial markets”, the Asean+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (AMRO) said in its 2026 Financial Stability Report published on Monday (Oct 5).
“A disorderly correction could therefore propagate through multiple channels – including lower technology exports, portfolio losses, capital outflows, refinancing pressure on leveraged technology and infrastructure firms, and weaker investor confidence,” it said.
The report comes amid growing investor concern about the AI boom, including the high valuation of tech companies, the surge in spending on chips and data centres, and circular financing deals in which companies appear to be funding each other.
Tech-related exports have been helping Asia withstand the impact of high energy prices and US tariffs.
Much of the physical production in the technology cycle takes place in Asia, from memory chips in South Korea to semiconductor assembly in Malaysia.
The region accounted for two-thirds of the growth in global AI-related trade, AMRO said.
Should AI demand suddenly fall short, a pullback in capital spending would undermine export revenues, investments and broader economic growth.
Some regional equity markets are also heavily concentrated on AI, such as South Korea, exposing them to a sharp correction in prices.
Other markets like Japan and Hong Kong have come to move closely in line with US AI and technology firms, meaning shocks could also be transmitted even absent a domestic trigger, according to AMRO.
As hyperscalers increasingly turn to borrowings to fund costly data center buildouts, higher leverage could amplify shocks if AI returns disappoint, the report said.
Opaque private credit markets and circular financing deals could worsen the instability.
“A sharp correction in AI-related financial assets could spill over to the broader financial system through forced deleveraging and tighter credit conditions,” AMRO said.
Central bankers around the world, from the Bank of England to the Monetary Authority of Singapore, have increasingly raised concerns about whether massive AI investments can be sustainable.
The technology has developed at breakneck speed, but stiff competition among developers, higher borrowing costs and growing pushback against data centres and AI’s security threats have raised concerns. BLOOMBERG

articles.title: Vietnam posts trade surplus after nine months of deficit - Thông tấn xã Việt Nam (TTXVN)
articles.summary: Vietnam posts trade surplus after nine months of deficit  Thông tấn xã Việt Nam (TTXVN)
articles.full_text:
| Transporting and loading commercial rice for export by the Southern Food Corporation. (Photo: VNA) | 
Hanoi (VNA) – Vietnam recorded a trade surplus in September after nine consecutive months of trade deficits, according to a socio-economic report for the third quarter and first nine months of 2026 released by the National Statistics Office under the Ministry of Finance on October 3.
The report showed that total export and import turnover reached 117.69 billion USD in September, up 7.3% from the previous month and 42.4% year-on-year. Notably, the goods trade balance returned to a surplus of 1.27 billion USD after nine consecutive months of deficit.
In the first nine months, total trade turnover reached 888.02 billion USD, up 30.4% year-on-year. Exports rose 24.5%, while imports increased 36.7%, resulting in a trade deficit of 19.42 billion USD.
Specifically, exports reached 59.48 billion USD in September, up 8.5% from the previous month and 39.1% year-on-year. Exports by the domestic economic sector increased 9.9%, while those by the foreign-invested sector, including crude oil, surged 46.5%.
In the third quarter, exports reached 167.85 billion USD, up 30.4% year-on-year and 17% from the second quarter.
In the first nine months, exports totalled 434.30 billion USD, up 24.5% year-on-year. The domestic economic sector contributed 83.89 billion USD, up 7.5% and accounting for 19.3% of total exports, while the foreign-invested sector, including crude oil, generated 350.41 billion USD, up 29.4% and accounting for 80.7%.
Thirty-five export items recorded turnover of more than 1 billion USD each, collectively making up 94.3% of total exports. Seven items posted export turnover of more than 10 billion USD each, accounting for 70.7% of the total.
Manufactured and processed industrial goods accounted for the largest share of exports at 392.79 billion USD, or 90.4%, followed by agricultural and forestry products at 30 billion USD (6.9%), seafood at 9.10 billion USD (2.1%), and fuels and minerals at 2.41 billion USD (0.6%).
Meanwhile, imports reached 58.21 billion USD in September, up 6% from the previous month and 45.8% year-on-year. Imports by the domestic economic sector rose 22.1%, while those by the foreign-invested sector increased 54.6%.
In the third quarter, imports totalled 170.33 billion USD, up 42.2% year-on-year and 8.8% from the second quarter.
In the first nine months, the figure reached 453.72 billion USD, up 36.7% year-on-year. The domestic economic sector accounted for 118.17 billion USD, up 23.5%, while the foreign-invested sector contributed 335.55 billion USD, up 42%.
Forty-five import items recorded turnover of more than 1 billion USD each, accounting for 94.5% of total imports, including six items with turnover exceeding 10 billion USD, which together accounted for 63.1%.
Production materials accounted for the overwhelming majority of imports, at 426.92 billion USD or 94.1%. Machinery, equipment, tools and spare parts made up 58.3%, while raw materials and fuels accounted for 35.8%. Consumer goods stood at 26.80 billion USD, or 5.9%.
In the first nine months, the US remained Vietnam's largest export market, with export turnover reaching 140.0 billion USD. China was Vietnam's largest import market, with import turnover of 187.34 billion USD.
Vietnam enjoyed a trade surplus of 122.62 billion USD with the US, up 23.8% year-on-year; 36.06 billion USD with the EU, up 25.3%; and 2.65 billion USD with Japan, up 85.9%.

articles.title: ‘Blessing in disguise’: Malaysia's Transport Minister Loke sees silver lining despite setbacks for his DAP - The Straits Times
articles.summary: ‘Blessing in disguise’: Malaysia's Transport Minister Loke sees silver lining despite setbacks for his DAP  The Straits TimesQuit as DAP sec-gen too over Najib’s conditional pardon, Loke told  Free Malaysia TodayLoke says resignation timing agreed with Anwar  NST OnlinePAS, Umno give Loke a poke: Quit first, Najib’s prison exit can wait  MalaysiakiniDAP keeps PH as preferred vehicle but leaves room for change ahead of GE16  thevibes.com

PUTRAJAYA – Anthony Loke should be leaving Malaysia’s Cabinet. Instead, the Democratic Action Party (DAP) secretary-general is strikingly upbeat about a party that has just suffered a string of electoral setbacks – including his own recent defeat in Negeri Sembilan.
“Negeri Sembilan’s defeat is basically a blessing in disguise for us,” the 49-year-old told The Straits Times in an exclusive interview on Oct 1. He noted that the UMNO-led state government, alongside Parti Islam SeMalaysia (PAS), remains mired in a royal crisis that they had promised to resolve upon coming to power under the Malay unity banner.
His optimism comes at a pivotal point for DAP, which has gone from perennial opposition to a key player in the federal government led by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim. Growing frustration among its core Chinese electorate has highlighted the limits of what it can achieve in a multi-party coalition.
Loke’s decision to leave the Cabinet over former prime minister Najib Razak’s house arrest illustrates the balancing act between staying in power and holding to principles the party says it cannot abandon.
Indeed, Loke should have cleared his desk after announcing on Sept 19 that he would quit the Cabinet in protest at Najib being allowed to serve the rest of his graft sentence related to the 1MDB scandal in his Kuala Lumpur mansion instead of Kajang Prison.
Instead, he has courted criticism after clarifying on Sept 29 that his resignation will only take effect once Najib pays the outstanding RM50 million (S$15.7 million) fine under the conditional house arrest order.
“Of course, people say that it’s an act, political, and so on,” Loke said, explaining that this was the agreed timeline with Anwar when he tendered his resignation. “But I’m sticking my head out – the moment he returns, I have to quit. I am not wishy-washy or dilly-dally. He goes home. I leave.”
The Sept 18 decision by the Pardons Board, chaired by Malaysia’s King, Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar of Johor, came despite Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) alliance campaigning to bring Najib and other perpetrators of the 1MDB scandal to justice. It is also the latest test for DAP, the backbone of Anwar’s coalition, which won 40 parliamentary seats at the 2022 general election.
DAP has also endured electoral setbacks in the Sabah, Johor and Negeri Sembilan state elections, with Loke himself losing Chennah – a seat he had held for three terms – on Aug 1.
Blessing in disguise
Loke remains confident that the Malay unity narrative pushed by UMNO and PAS will not be sustainable. The two major Malay-Muslim parties joined forces in Negeri Sembilan to secure control of the state administration, unseating PH, of which DAP is the largest component party.
“Negeri Sembilan’s defeat is basically a blessing in disguise for us. They (UMNO-PAS) talked about Malay unity and forming a formidable state government to resolve the royal impasse. What decision did they make? They dethroned the state ruler.
“Right now, Malays elsewhere in the entire country can see that an UMNO-PAS government did this. So that’s why I said DAP is being spared this burden right now. In a way, the Malay unity momentum cannot necessarily be sustained in terms of electoral trends,” he told ST.
The dispute centres on the contested removal of state ruler Muhriz Munawir, with competing claims over the legitimacy of the move.
Growing disappointment
DAP still commands strong support among Chinese voters, but that alone cannot deliver federal power.
Growing disappointment among Chinese voters – the core electorate that propelled DAP and PH into power in the 2022 general election – remains a persistent headache for Loke.
Political scientist Bridget Welsh estimated 95 per cent of Chinese voters backed PH in 2022, with a 69% voter turnout.
In the subsequent state elections, PH’s Chinese support remained high at 97 per cent in Negeri Sembilan with a 67 per cent turnout, but dropped to 80 per cent in Johor alongside a lower turnout of 63 per cent.
Loke, stressing that DAP will never take Chinese support “for granted”, noted that Malaysian political reality demands consensus-building among coalition partners, meaning DAP’s vision can rarely be realised in full.
“We know sometimes it’s frustrating to be in this kind of situation, but that is the reality of Malaysian politics.
“There is no way for DAP to form a government on its own without working with others. This is a reality we must accept: We can only push as far as possible, relying on objective and persuasive arguments to get things done within the system,” he explained.
Full recognition of the Unified Examination Certificate (UEC) for public university entry remains a priority for DAP, but one that is still unresolved.
Under the Anwar administration’s 2026 policy, UEC students are required to meet Bahasa Melayu and History requirements under the national examination framework, while access to public universities remains subject to specified conditions.
For DAP, the long-championed UEC issue illustrates the limits of what it can achieve inside a coalition government.
DAP is at a pivotal point, but staying in government does not mean the party will “sacrifice everything” to retain power.
Drawing a firm line
For Loke, there are limits to pragmatism. He drew a firm line over Najib’s house arrest, while seeking to avoid a mass resignation by DAP ministers and deputy ministers.
Loke officially tendered his resignation as Transport Minister to Anwar on Sept 28, following his announcement to the DAP Central Executive Committee.
“As the leader of the party, I must demonstrate leadership and show our voters that we hold fast to certain principles,” Loke explained.
“Power is important, but that does not mean we will sacrifice everything just to retain position and office.”
With the next federal election due by February 2028, DAP will need to rebuild beyond its traditional support base while holding on to its core Chinese electorate. Loke believes it can still command about 80 per cent of Chinese voter support, based on recent state-election results, though he acknowledged that “90 per cent is a tall order.”
Asked about Parti Bersama Malaysia (Bersama), a splinter party led by former Parti Keadilan Rakyat (PKR) figures that has sought to appeal to disaffected urban PH voters, Loke argued that third forces and idealistic parties rarely sustain momentum in Malaysian politics.
“The most recent example would be the Malaysian United Democratic Alliance (MUDA). They put forward super idealistic objectives, fresh candidates, young people, professionals, and so on.
“But after the election, they are nowhere to be seen.”
Bersama fielded 15 candidates in the July Johor state polls, all of whom lost their deposits. The party nevertheless plans to contest the coming Melaka state election, which must be called before Nov 22.
Door remains open
If DAP wants to remain in federal government after GE16, it may again have to work with parties unpopular with parts of its grassroots.
Many DAP supporters continue to be deeply opposed to PAS because of its Islamist politics, while distrust of UMNO and Bersatu persists over their previous and current roles in coalition governments.
PAS is the largest single party in Malaysia’s parliament with 43 out of 222 seats, leading the opposition Perikatan Nasional (PN) coalition.
For example, Melaka DAP chairman Khoo Poay Tiong declined a dinner hosted by Bersatu on Oct 1, attended by other PH leaders, saying DAP was not yet ready to work with the party in the coming state election.
Still, Loke insisted he has not ruled out working with any potential partners, pointing to DAP’s historic decision to cooperate with UMNO following the 2022 general election to form the Anwar-led federal government.
“I don’t close my doors to anyone.
“I hold this belief that we have come to a point that politics has to be agile. Of course, not without any principle or any precondition, because it depends on the circumstances what is best for the country to move forward.”
The August referendum on whether DAP should remain in the Anwar administration also underscored the debate within the party over its relationship with the unity government.
Loke did not rule out the possibility of DAP contesting the next federal election on its own rather than as part of PH.
“As much as possible, I want to preserve the PH coalition.
“But again, our electoral strategy needs to be reviewed from time to time. What is the best strategy – not only for DAP, but for our partners as well?
“I can only answer that when parliament is dissolved.”

On October 2, 2026, in Cape Town, Republic of South Africa, the Forum on Prospects for Economic, Trade, and Investment Cooperation between Vietnam and South Africa took place with the participation of leaders of the Vietnamese National Assembly, representatives of the Ministry of Industry and Trade, the Vietnamese Embassy in South Africa, the Western Cape Tourism, Trade and Investment Promotion Agency (WESGRO), relevant agencies, and the business communities of both countries.
The forum was one of the activities within the framework of the official visit of the high-level delegation of the Vietnamese National Assembly to Cape Town, the legislative capital of South Africa. Delegates focused on exchanging views on the business environment, trade and investment opportunities, relevant policies and regulations, and areas with significant potential for cooperation.
Integrating Strategic Partnerships into the Economy
In his opening remarks at the Forum, Vice Chairman of the National Assembly Nguyen Hong Dien emphasized that over the past 30 years, the friendship and cooperation between Vietnam and South Africa have developed in a substantive and effective manner. The upgrading of relations to a Strategic Partnership in November 2025 opens a new framework for cooperation with a long-term vision and higher demands for quality and effectiveness. Economic, trade, and investment cooperation is one of the important pillars of this framework.

According to the Vice Chairman of the National Assembly, bilateral trade turnover is projected to reach approximately US$1.3 billion in 2025; and over US$1.7 billion in the first seven months of 2026, a 45% increase compared to the same period last year. South Africa is currently Vietnam's second largest trading partner and its largest export market in Africa; while Vietnam is South Africa's fifth largest trading partner in the ASEAN region.
However, these results are still considered to be below the potential and strengths of the two economies, as well as the framework of the Strategic Partnership.
Structurally, the two economies have complementary advantages. South Africa has strengths in resources, industry, services, finance, and its gateway location to the African market. Vietnam has strengths in manufacturing, processing, agriculture , technology, electronics, telecommunications, international trade, and experience in participating in value chains.
Based on that foundation, the two sides can expand cooperation in high value-added areas such as processing and manufacturing industries, digital transformation , artificial intelligence, green economy, renewable energy, mining and mineral processing, high-tech agriculture, and supporting industries.
One of the issues emphasized by Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly Nguyen Hong Dien is building a favorable legal environment to transform cooperation potential into concrete projects and capital flows. Accordingly, businesses need an investment, production, and business environment with clear, transparent, stable, and predictable regulations; simplified procedures; reduced compliance costs; and guaranteed protection of their legitimate rights and interests.
Trade promotion paves the way for businesses.
From a trade promotion perspective, Mr. Vu Ba Phu, Director of the Trade Promotion Department, Ministry of Industry and Trade , introduced the developments in the Vietnamese economy as well as the opportunities that the Vietnamese market can offer to South African businesses.
Mr. Vu Ba Phu, Director of the Trade Promotion Department, delivered a speech at the forum.
According to Mr. Vu Ba Phu, in the last five years, the level of integration of the Vietnamese economy into international trade and investment has become increasingly deep and broad. The scale of goods trade increased from approximately US$668.5 billion in 2021 to approximately US$930 billion in 2025. Registered FDI capital in 2025 is expected to reach approximately US$38.42 billion, and implemented capital is projected to reach US$27.62 billion.
These results demonstrate Vietnam's increasing role as a manufacturing and export hub in the region. This also provides a basis for Vietnam and South Africa to explore complementary cooperation models, ranging from raw material and input product supply, deep processing cooperation, and the development of supporting industries to expanding markets for each country's strong products.
The Trade Promotion Agency is ready to act as a bridge, supporting businesses in both countries to explore markets, find partners, and implement specific cooperation opportunities.
International trade promotion programs and events such as Vietnam Expo, Vietnam Foodexpo, VIATT, Vietnam Global International Fair, along with business networking and exchange programs, are presented as channels for South African businesses to gain deeper access to the Vietnamese market.
According to Mr. Vu Ba Phu, Vietnam hopes that South African trade promotion agencies, associations, and businesses will participate more deeply in programs in Vietnam, from exhibitions and B2B trade to finding suppliers and investment partners, and building long-term cooperative relationships.
Conversely, WESGRO states that South Africa is Africa's most industrialized and diversified economy, with a size of $363 billion, a market of 63 million people, and preferential access to African markets through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
The Western Cape province, in particular, has been identified as having potential for cooperation with Vietnamese businesses in the fields of renewable energy, green hydrogen, electric vehicles, battery manufacturing, high-tech agriculture, agricultural product processing, logistics, and information technology services. WESGRO has also built the Cape Trade Portal, connecting more than 2,100 exporters in the region with buyers worldwide.
Energy and business connectivity
One notable topic at the Forum was the prospect of cooperation in the energy sector, including coal trade between Vietnam and South Africa.
Mr. Trinh Duc Duy, Deputy Director of the Department of Energy and Petroleum, Ministry of Industry and Trade, stated that in the orientation of ensuring energy security, serving socio-economic development and implementing energy transition, Vietnam highly appreciates the role of international cooperation in the energy sector.
According to discussions at the Forum, Vietnam's coal import needs remain significant in the coming period, while South Africa has strengths in coal mining and export, and possesses a large-scale infrastructure system to support exports. Both sides could explore expanding cooperation by diversifying supply sources, strengthening business connections, exchanging market information, and gradually exploring the possibility of investment cooperation.
Representatives from the Ministry of Industry and Trade requested that South Africa facilitate direct contact between Vietnamese businesses and reputable coal suppliers, support access to market information, and conduct surveys and research on investment opportunities in coal mining, processing, and supply in South Africa. This is identified as a complementary area of cooperation, consistent with the requirements for ensuring energy security and diversifying the supply chain.
In addition to policy dialogue, the Forum allocated time for businesses from both countries to exchange information on needs, cooperation opportunities, and practical issues in accessing the market.
Q&A session with businesses
The Q&A session with businesses facilitates the transformation of information exchanged at the Forum into concrete connections, ranging from finding partners, suppliers, and customers to researching investment opportunities.
The upgrading of Vietnam-South Africa relations to a Strategic Partnership creates a further foundation for the two countries to expand cooperation in many areas. In particular, economics, trade, and investment continue to be important areas, with increasingly active participation from the business community.

articles.title: Vietnam Pushes IPO Reforms to Boost Stock Market Listings - briefasia.com

articles.full_text:
New Rules Target Listing Barriers
Vietnam's Ministry of Finance has submitted draft regulations to the government that would directly link initial public offerings to stock exchange listing requirements, a move designed to reduce procedural friction for companies seeking public capital.
The proposed framework eliminates several administrative steps that previously separated the IPO process from exchange admission, according to the ministry. Under the new structure, companies completing an IPO would face a clearer path to listing, cutting the timeline between raising capital and trading debut.
The ministry is positioning the reforms as part of a wider strategy to expand the supply of investable assets in Vietnam's equity markets. Current market depth remains constrained by a relatively small pool of listed companies compared to the size of the economy, a gap that has limited institutional participation and benchmark index composition.
Focus on Corporate Governance
A second pillar of the initiative targets large, well-governed enterprises that have remained private despite meeting the scale and financial criteria for public listing. The ministry is developing incentives to bring these firms onto the exchange, though specific measures have not yet been disclosed.
Vietnam's stock market has historically attracted small and mid-cap companies, while many of the country's largest corporations - including state-owned enterprises and family-controlled conglomerates - have avoided public listings. The ministry's emphasis on governance standards signals an intent to raise the quality threshold for new entrants, rather than simply increasing the quantity of listed names.
The reforms arrive as Vietnam seeks to position its capital markets for an upgrade in MSCI's emerging market classification, a designation that would unlock substantial foreign institutional inflows. Current market infrastructure, including settlement systems and foreign ownership limits, has been cited by index providers as needing further development.
Product Diversification on the Agenda
Beyond equity listings, the ministry outlined plans to diversify the range of tradable instruments available to investors. Vietnam's exchanges currently offer limited derivative products and lack several asset classes common in more developed regional markets, including real estate investment trusts and exchange-traded funds tracking sector indices.
The ministry has not provided a timeline for parliamentary review of the IPO regulations, though submission to the government typically precedes a multi-month legislative process. Implementation would require coordination with the State Securities Commission, which oversees listing standards and exchange operations.
Market participants have long identified the listing process as a bottleneck. The current system requires separate approvals for the IPO itself and subsequent exchange admission, creating uncertainty for companies and underwriters about timing and final terms. The proposed integration would align Vietnam more closely with practices in Thailand and Malaysia, where IPO approval automatically confers listing eligibility.
Regional Context
The reforms come as Southeast Asian exchanges compete for new listings amid a regional slowdown in IPO activity. Singapore and Malaysia have both introduced measures in the past year to attract mid-sized companies, while Thailand has eased profitability requirements for technology firms.
Vietnam's benchmark VN-Index has traded in a narrow range over the past eighteen months, with foreign investors remaining net sellers for much of the period. Domestic retail investors continue to dominate trading volume, accounting for more than 80 per cent of daily turnover.
The ministry's emphasis on governance and market quality suggests a shift from earlier policies that prioritised rapid expansion of listed company numbers. That approach, pursued through the mid-2020s, resulted in a wave of small-cap listings that struggled to maintain liquidity and attracted limited institutional interest.
Whether the new framework will succeed in drawing Vietnam's largest private firms to the public markets remains an open question. Many of these companies have accessed capital through private placements and bank lending, avoiding the disclosure requirements and shareholder scrutiny that come with exchange listing.

articles.title: Japan Semiconductor Firm Breaks Ground on 20-Hectare Batangas Plant - briefasia.com

articles.full_text:
Second Site for Established Player
A Japanese semiconductor manufacturer will break ground in November on a 20-hectare manufacturing facility at the LIMA Estate in Batangas, according to Aboitiz Economic Estates. The project represents the firm's second Philippine location, building on an existing presence elsewhere in the country.
Rafael Fernandez de Mesa, president and chief executive of Aboitiz Economic Estates, described the investor as "one of the bigger global companies from Japan" but did not disclose its identity. The groundbreaking ceremony is scheduled for mid-November.
The expansion follows a pattern Aboitiz Economic Estates has observed across its industrial park network: roughly half of new tenants each year are existing Philippine-based manufacturers adding capacity. "That tells you that those investors are happy with the Philippines," De Mesa said.
Food and Electronics Pipeline
A foreign food manufacturer is preparing to establish a 12-hectare facility at the company's TARI Estate in Tarlac, with construction expected to begin in early 2027. The firm is currently completing registration formalities with Philippine authorities.
TARI Estate's initial tenants have concentrated in food and beverage processing. De Mesa said the company anticipates the next wave of locators will mirror LIMA Estate's broader industrial mix, which includes electronics and semiconductor operations alongside other sectors.
Regional Corridor Momentum
The Philippine government has promoted the Luzon Economic Corridor and initiatives such as Pax Silica to attract technology manufacturing investment. De Mesa cited these policy frameworks as potential accelerators for demand that has already been "consistent over the last 10 years."
He emphasised that capturing increased investment flows requires readiness across three dimensions: land availability, utility infrastructure, and skilled labour supply. Industrial park operators and government agencies must coordinate to ensure all three are in place when manufacturers evaluate site options.
Streamlined Permitting
Aboitiz Economic Estates and the Philippine Economic Zone Authority signed a memorandum of understanding to extend the EaseBiz programme, a joint effort launched in 2022 to simplify registration and operational setup for zone tenants. Since the programme's formalisation in 2025, it has supported six investor registration cases; prior to formalisation, it assisted more than two dozen applicants.
The next phase will align locator-support workflows with PEZA's One Portal System. Tereso Panga, PEZA director general, said the agency has automated 80 per cent of its permitting processes and aims to reach full automation by 2027, positioning PEZA among the first Philippine government bodies to operate entirely cashless and paperless.
"PEZA remains committed to enhancing ease of doing business in our ecozones so that investor confidence translates into concrete projects, quality jobs and increased exports," Panga said.
Philippines in the Chip Map
The semiconductor investments landing in Batangas and Tarlac come as electronics assembly and test operations dominate Philippine manufacturing exports. The country hosts back-end semiconductor work for a range of multinational firms, and the announced Japanese facility will deepen that presence.
Southeast Asia has emerged as a secondary destination for chip-related capital expenditure as companies seek alternatives to concentrated manufacturing footprints in Taiwan and South Korea. Vietnam, Malaysia, and Singapore have captured the bulk of regional investment, but the Philippines is positioning itself for assembly, packaging, and test operations that require large workforces and stable utility supply.
The 20-hectare scale of the Batangas project suggests a substantial commitment. Industrial estates in the region typically allocate sites of that size to anchor tenants planning multi-year expansions or integrated production lines.
Aboitiz Economic Estates operates industrial parks across Luzon and has positioned LIMA Estate as a hub for electronics and precision manufacturing. The estate's proximity to the Port of Batangas provides logistics advantages for firms shipping components and finished goods within Asia-Pacific supply chains.
De Mesa's observation that half of new locators come from within the existing Philippine network points to a maturing industrial ecosystem. When established manufacturers expand rather than relocate, it indicates stable operating conditions, reliable supplier networks, and confidence in long-term policy settings.
The food sector investment at TARI Estate reflects separate diversification within Philippine industrial parks. Consumer goods manufacturers are expanding regional production capacity to serve Southeast Asian markets, leveraging the Philippines' young workforce and growing domestic consumption base.
Both investments underscore the role of private industrial estates in Philippine economic development. With public infrastructure often constrained, private operators that bundle land, utilities, and regulatory support can attract multinational capital more effectively than unserviced zones.

From production to value creation in Vietnam
Opening a series of inspiring speeches themed "The World Joins Hands in Action with Vietnam," Mr. Na Ki Hong, General Director of Samsung Vietnam, stated that the role of FDI enterprises should not only be measured by factory size or export turnover, but also by their ability to contribute to the development of domestic technological capabilities.
According to the General Director of Samsung Vietnam, the crucial question is how many Vietnamese engineers are involved in creating the products and how many Vietnamese businesses have the capacity to become suppliers.
One example cited by the General Director of Samsung Vietnam is the team of engineers at the Samsung Vietnam Research and Development Center in Hanoi who participated in developing software for global products. Vietnamese became one of the 13 languages supported when the Galaxy S24 Ultra was launched. Subsequently, the Vietnamese engineering team continued to contribute to subsequent generations of products.
Alongside its research and development activities, Samsung implements numerous programs to train technology personnel and support Vietnamese businesses in improving their production capabilities. In particular, the Smart Factory Development Consulting Program has partnered with 91 businesses and trained 201 Vietnamese experts.
If products are assembled only in Vietnam, their value primarily lies in the scale of production. It is only when Vietnamese engineers directly solve an R&D problem and the results are used in a global product that true technological capability is formed and retained.
According to the General Director of Samsung Vietnam, the company focuses on two pillars: developing technological talent and enhancing the innovation capacity of domestic businesses.
In 2026, more than 2,900 teams participated in Samsung Solve for Tomorrow. The Samsung Innovation Campus continues to train students in artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, big data, and semiconductors. From 2012 to the present, Samsung has invested approximately 180 billion VND in university cooperation programs, research, and talent training.
In the business sector, the Smart Factory Development Consulting Program, in coordination with the Ministry of Industry and Trade and local authorities, has supported 91 businesses and trained 201 Vietnamese experts. At a plastics company in Bac Ninh, the application of a data management solution helped increase the plan completion rate from 80% to 92%, while the error rate decreased from 12% to 0.5%.
According to Mr. Na Ki Hong, Vietnam already has a large-scale, high-tech manufacturing base and needs to continue increasing the value created domestically.
"The next chapter needs to be written with more Vietnamese engineers participating in core R&D tasks; more Vietnamese businesses mastering data, processes, and standards; and more technological value being created, disseminated, and retained within the Vietnamese economy ," he said.
Bringing Vietnamese knowledge and culture into the digital world.
Under the theme "Overseas Vietnamese experts and intellectuals promote the flow of knowledge and technology to Vietnam," Christopher Nguyen, founder and CEO of Aitomatic, shared his story about bringing the Vietnamese language and knowledge into the digital environment.
According to Christopher Nguyen, about 34 years ago, the effort to bring the Vietnamese language into the digital world began with a small group of people. Since then, the development of the internet and digital platforms has connected more and more Vietnamese people with the world.
Today, children can use phones, access information, and connect with many places around the world. The development of digital platforms and content creators has contributed to the formation of a vast body of knowledge, providing a foundation for people to plan their future.
This also serves as a source of data for artificial intelligence to learn from. Increasingly, knowledge is being created and stored in the digital environment, becoming a data source for machines to learn from, while also being supplemented by the experience and expertise of engineers.
The founder and CEO of Aitomatic believes that Vietnam possesses many values that the world needs, from language and culture to knowledge and a worldview.
While the Vietnamese language previously had limited presence in the digital space, the development of AI is opening up opportunities for Vietnamese knowledge to be digitized, disseminated, and contribute to the global knowledge base.
According to him, AI needs not only data from a single language but also knowledge resources specific to each country and community. Many countries are developing AI systems based on their own data, culture, and knowledge. This also presents an opportunity for Vietnam to build AI capabilities based on its unique values.
In this context, the concept of sovereignty no longer means simply separating or protecting individual resources. Digital sovereignty also lies in the ability to collaboratively create, share, and contribute knowledge to bring value to the community.
Based on efforts to introduce the Vietnamese language into the digital world decades ago, Christopher Nguyen believes that today's technological platform has opened up greater possibilities, helping Vietnamese language, knowledge, and culture enter the AI era and build a broader digital future.
Lessons learned from Singapore's experience in building an innovation ecosystem.
Sharing his views on "Policy Mechanisms to Promote Innovation and Suggestions for Vietnam," Edward Lim, Country Director of NUS Enterprise, argued that an innovation ecosystem cannot be formed from a single program but requires the simultaneous development of talent, support mechanisms, and capital, creating a continuous journey from research to market.
According to Edward Lim, since 1991, Singapore has committed over S$125 billion to research and innovation, including S$37 billion for RIE2030 over the next five years. Public investment in this sector is maintained at approximately 1% of GDP.
Funding is used to support the entire technology journey, from its inception to market launch, thereby minimizing risks at each stage. The National Research Foundation (NRF) of Singapore is responsible for coordinating the plan and funding, while universities and businesses are the implementing entities.
In addition, national programs for developing entrepreneurial capacity within the research community, such as National GRIP, have also been implemented.
Citing the case of the biotechnology startup Forte Biotech, Edward Lim said the company was founded by two former NUS students, one of whom is Vietnamese. Through the GRIP program, the team's research was developed based on licensed patents, received funding from NUS, and brought the solution to Vietnam to provide rapid testing and diagnosis solutions for aquatic diseases, especially shrimp diseases, directly in aquaculture ponds.
Between 2018 and 2023, corporate R&D spending in Singapore increased from S$5.5 billion to S$9 billion. According to Edward Lim, it is crucial to consider how much additional R&D resources and activity from the private sector can be mobilized by the government's investment.
Drawing from Singapore's experience, he offered three suggestions for Vietnam: promoting talent mobility so that international knowledge and experience can be applied domestically; building a seamless support system from idea generation and testing to customers and markets; and using public capital as a catalyst to reduce risks for startups in their early stages.
He cited programs like UniVentures and 84X as examples of how to connect founders and startups with the market and real-world business problems.
"For Vietnam to move further up the global value chain, part of the answer lies in whether 'the next step is prepared before the current step is completed'," Edward Lim emphasized.
Bringing Vietnamese chips from design to market.
Under the theme "Pioneering innovative startups stepping into the global market," Mr. Ta Hong Phuc, Deputy General Director of Hyphen Deux, shared the story of bringing Vietnamese chips from design to market-ready products.
According to him, from a business perspective, the innovation system needs to be viewed from a very specific point: technology must travel all the way to the product and the customer. For the semiconductor industry, this journey is much longer than a single announced technical milestone.
A year ago, at Innovate Vietnam 2025, Hyphen Deux announced that the HDx32U, a microcontroller chip designed by Vietnamese engineers, had completed its tape-out, marking a transition from design to manufacturing.
"However, for us, tape-out is just the beginning," said Mr. Ta Hong Phuc.
Next come the steps of manufacturing, packaging, testing, integration onto the board, real-world operation, and software refinement. More importantly, the product must be used by the customer.
According to him, when choosing new components, businesses need stability, supporting documentation and software, a long-term supply, and the ability to control risks.
Therefore, semiconductor capability should not be measured solely by the number of chips designed or the number of completed tape-out projects, but rather by the number of actual products using Vietnamese chips, the number of engineers mastering the process, and the number of customers who continue to place orders.

The global flat rack container market represents a specialized but indispensable segment of the intermodal freight industry, engineered to carry heavy, oversized, and irregularly shaped cargo that standard dry containers cannot accommodate. As of 2026, the market is emerging from a period of post-pandemic volatility into a more stable yet strategically segmented growth phase. Demand is closely tied to global capital expenditure cycles, particularly in construction, energy, and heavy machinery sectors. The energy transition, especially the rapid expansion of wind and solar installations, is creating new demand for flat racks to transport turbine blades, nacelles, and transformer units.
Simultaneously, infrastructure stimulus programs in Asia-Pacific and North America are boosting shipments of construction equipment and industrial project cargo. However, the market faces headwinds from steel price volatility, container availability imbalances, and geopolitical trade disruptions. This report provides a data-driven analysis of the market's structure, key drivers, restraints, and competitive landscape, with a forecast to 2035.
It covers product types including collapsible, fixed-end, gooseneck, platform-based, reinforced deck, and sidewall flat racks, and examines end-use sectors such as heavy machinery, construction, oversized cargo logistics, industrial project cargo, and renewable energy. The analysis is designed for manufacturers, lessors, logistics providers, and investors seeking a consistent, transparent view of market dynamics and a clear definition of product scope.
The baseline scenario for the flat rack container market from 2026 to 2035 anticipates moderate but steady growth, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 3.8%, bringing the market index to 145 by 2035 (2025=100). This outlook assumes a gradual recovery in global trade volumes, continued investment in renewable energy infrastructure, and stable but elevated steel prices. Demand will be uneven across regions, with Asia-Pacific leading in both production and consumption, followed by Europe and North America. The market will benefit from the ongoing shift toward modular construction and the transport of oversized components for wind farms, which require specialized flat rack solutions.
However, restraints such as container availability, high logistics costs, and trade tensions will temper growth. The aftermarket and leasing segments are expected to gain share as operators seek flexible capacity. Technological advancements in lightweight materials and collapsible designs will improve efficiency and reduce repositioning costs. articles.title: Food prices rise by nearly 6% annually due to wars and climate phenomena - noticiasambientales.com
articles.summary: Food prices rise by nearly 6% annually due to wars and climate phenomena  noticiasambientales.com
articles.full_text:
The FAO food price index reached 136 points in September, with a monthly increase of 1.5% and an annual rise of 5.8%. The advance was related to logistical problems, trade tensions, and adverse weather phenomena.
In particular, disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the Black Sea increased uncertainty about transportation and energy costs. Additionally, various climatic events reduced the prospects for production of some crops.
Thus, a localized disruption can spread through international supply chains and end up impacting consumer prices, especially in countries dependent on imports.
Cereals bear much of the pressure
The cereal price index increased by 5.1% during September and was 17.2% above the record of the same month in 2025. Within this group, wheat rose by 6.3%, while corn advanced by 5.6%.
In the case of wheat, logistical restrictions in the Black Sea region and drought recorded in some areas of North America before planting contributed to the increase.
On the other hand, corn was conditioned by the prospects of lower yields in the United States, reduced export availability from Brazil, and trade difficulties in the Black Sea. Additionally, its use as a raw material for biofuels adds pressure on demand.
Vegetable oils also increased by 0.9%, mainly due to the rising cost of palm oil and concerns about production in Southeast Asia. Sugar, meanwhile, rose by 6.1%, while meat fell by 1.1% and dairy decreased by 0.1%.
Lower production and greater climatic uncertainty
The FAO forecasts that global cereal production will reach 2.979 million tons in 2026, 2.1% less than in 2025. Although it would be the second most abundant harvest recorded, the decline highlights the increasing variability of production conditions.
Likewise, global cereal trade could decrease by 3.5%, to 505.8 million tons, mainly due to restrictions on Black Sea maritime routes.
Added to this are high transportation tariffs, firmer fertilizer markets, and logistical problems. Moreover, the strengthening of El Niño introduces new risks for agriculture, especially in South and Southeast Asia.
What is food insecurity and what factors cause it?
Food insecurity occurs when people do not have regular access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious food to maintain a healthy life. Therefore, it does not only depend on the availability of food but also on being able to obtain it in a stable and economically accessible manner.
Among its main factors are conflicts, economic crises, poverty, inequalities in access, trade disruptions, and climate emergencies. When these elements coincide, families may reduce the quantity or quality of the food they consume.
In this context, climate change is becoming increasingly important because it can alter rainfall, temperatures, and agricultural yields. At the same time, droughts, floods, and heatwaves can deteriorate soils and crops, while rising energy, fertilizer, and transportation costs increase the costs of the entire chain.
The evolution of international prices thus constitutes a relevant signal to anticipate possible difficulties. The FAO itself uses internal price monitoring systems as early warning tools for situations that may affect food security.
Finally, strengthening resilient agricultural systems, diversifying supply sources, and reducing vulnerability to climatic events is essential to prevent a production or logistical crisis from becoming a food emergency.

Speaking at the forum, Associate Professor Dr. Nguyen Tien Hoang, Head of the Finance and Banking Faculty, Van Lang University, stated that the wealth management market in Vietnam is facing strong growth opportunities.
According to statistics from McKinsey & Company (2023), the size of personal financial assets in Vietnam reached US$360 billion in 2022, and is expected to reach US$600 billion in 2027 (with a growth rate of approximately US$65-75 billion/year).
This scale is equivalent to approximately 90% of the national GDP, and the actual potential is even greater, as the statistics do not include key non-financial asset classes of Vietnamese people such as real estate and gold.

"The market is currently witnessing a fundamental shift from both sides. On the customer side, demand has moved beyond individual, integrated financial products such as deposits, insurance, and stocks, towards a holistic solution linked to the individual's ecosystem and lifecycle," Associate Professor Dr. Nguyen Tien Hoang commented.
Dr. Bui Van Huy, General Director of FIDT Investment Consulting and Asset Management Joint Stock Company, said that while a few years ago the market was still asking "What is Wealth?", now the focus has shifted to building and operating an effective Wealth management model suitable for Vietnam's conditions.
Asset managementis no longer just a family-level issue.
According to Dr. Bui Van Huy, the development of asset management models in Vietnam is not only related to the financial needs of individual families but also linked to larger issues of the market and the economy . However, the role of the asset management industry is still not fully recognized.
He argued that capital flows in the economy should not only come from gold or foreign currency, but need to be transformed into strategic capital flows. If a developed asset management market is established in Vietnam, this capital flow could have a significant impact on the economy, similar to attracting more foreign capital.
In the context of Vietnam's emerging needs for asset management and allocation, the issue of estate management is no longer just a family-level matter but can be viewed from an economic perspective, from micro to macro levels.
In the coming period, the wealth management industry in Vietnam is expected to continue to evolve and grow, as the wealthy and middle classes continue to expand.

While the economy needs large-scale, long-term capital, traditional funding channels are limited. Conversely, household and private sector assets are accumulating rapidly. The gap lies in the fact that resources and investment needs exist, but the mechanisms for connecting them are not yet adequate.
Dr. Bui Van Huy also believes that the estate management market in Vietnam still has some gaps that need to be addressed, such as limited products for the estate management market, an incomplete official legal framework for the estate management industry, and the lack of a professional certification system and common standards for consultants.
He stated that FIDT has put forward recommendations to contribute to the development of a formal legal framework for this field. Simultaneously, the development of professional certifications and common standards for consultants is also considered one of the issues that need to be addressed to fill market gaps.

IPOH - A 49-year-old housewife was charged in the Magistrate's Court here on Friday (Oct 2) with the murder of her 70-year-old bedridden mother in Menglembu last week.
Chew Loong Thye indicated that she understood the charge after it was read to her in Cantonese before Magistrate Norizan Riduan, NST reported.
No plea was recorded as capital murder offences fall under the exclusive jurisdiction of the High Court.
Chew is accused of murdering her mother, Ching Lai Kheng, at a house in Taman Wang, Menglembu, between 7.15pm and 7.30pm on Sept 27.
The charge was framed under Section 302 of the Penal Code, which provides for the death penalty or imprisonment of between 30 and 40 years upon conviction.
During the proceedings, Norizan asked Chew whether she had been regularly taking her prescribed psychiatric medication, to which she answered affirmatively.
The court subsequently ordered Chew to undergo a formal psychiatric evaluation and for an assessment report to be prepared in accordance with Section 342(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code.
Deputy Public Prosecutor Ainin Sofiya Azlaini informed the court that pathology and toxicology reports remain pending and confirmed that no bail was being offered, as murder is a non-bailable offence. Chew was unrepresented.
The court fixed Nov 22 for case mention and the submission of the psychiatric report.
Perak police chief Datuk Mohd Alwi Zainal Abidin previously confirmed on Sept 28 that the victim was discovered with a fatal stab wound to her chest.
